questions.problem: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=3{t}^{2}-9t+1$, where $t>0$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of increasing $x,$ then its velocity is positive. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}-9t+1) \\  & =6t-9\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x$, we solve $v(t)>0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & >0 \\ 6t-9 & >0 \\ 6t & >9 \\ t & >\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of increasing $x$ is $t\in (\frac{3}{2},\infty ).$

questions.problem: The displacement $s,$ in meters, relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by $s(t)=(3t+1){e}^{-t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time measured in seconds. Determine the time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x.$
questions.worked_solution:
If the particle moves in the direction of decreasing $x,$ then its velocity is negative. 

First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((3t+1){e}^{-t}) \\  & =(2-3t){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate time intervals in which the particle is moving in the direction of decreasing $x$, we solve the inequality $v(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & <0 \\ (2-3t){e}^{-t} & <0 \\ 2-3t & <0 \\ 3t & >2 \\ t & >\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the time interval in which the particle is moving to the direction of decreasing $x$ is $t\in (\frac{2}{3},\infty ).$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+t\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t={e}^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v({e}^{-3/2}) & =2({e}^{-3/2})\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-3/2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =2{e}^{-3/2}(-\frac{3}{2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =-2{e}^{-3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$
